questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Forces Shaping the Earth's Surface' refers to.
questions.a: The earth's surface is constantly shaped by two families of forces: internal forces from within the earth that raise mountains and trigger earthquakes and volcanoes, and external forces of weathering and erosion that wear the relief down and redeposit it.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Forces Shaping the Earth's Surface'.
questions.a: Building forces within, wearing forces without: the landscape is their tug-of-war.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Forces Shaping the Earth's Surface' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 2 (source: iest102.txt opening sections (what shapes the earth's surface))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Weathering and Erosion' refers to.
questions.a: Weathering breaks rocks in place through sun, water, frost and living things; erosion carries the broken material away through rivers, wind, glaciers and sea waves, depositing it as plains, deltas and sand dunes elsewhere.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Weathering and Erosion'.
questions.a: Weathering breaks, erosion carries, deposition builds - the three-step landform cycle.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Weathering and Erosion' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 2 (source: iest102.txt sections on weathering, erosion and deposition)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Landforms and Human Life' refers to.
questions.a: Mountains, plateaus and plains each host distinct human activities - farming in plains, herding and tourism in mountains, mining on plateaus - while hazards like earthquakes demand that settlements respect the forces shaping the land.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Landforms and Human Life'.
questions.a: Landform decides livelihood: plains farm, mountains herd, plateaus mine.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Landforms and Human Life' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 2 (source: iest102.txt sections on landforms and human adaptation)
